articles.title: Women reach orgasm more often alone, but partnered orgasms are more closely tied to sexual satisfaction
articles.summary: In a survey of nearly 28,000 period-tracking app users, women reported reaching orgasm more often during solo sex than with a partner. Yet it was partnered orgasm frequency, not solo orgasm frequency, that was linked to greater overall sexual satisfaction.

articles.title: Feed recommendations are the most common way teens encounter self-harm content
articles.summary: About one in three English secondary school students had come across self-harm content online in the past month. Most never went looking for it; the content typically appeared in their social media feeds.

articles.title: Phase-based Edge Coupling: Modeling Overlapping Functional Architectures and High-Order Edge-to-Edge Interactions in EEG Networks
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.32286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Network neuroscience has traditionally relied on node-centric approaches, which are inherently limited in capturing the brain's overlapping functional architectures and higher-order edge-to-edge interactions. The emerging edge-centric paradigm addresses this gap by shifting the analytical unit from nodes to edges. However, while edge-centric models have been established for DTI and fMRI, comparable EEG methodologies have yet to be developed. articles.title: Frequent cannabis use linked to higher odds of nighttime breathing problems
articles.summary: A new study links cannabis use to loud snoring and breathing pauses during sleep, with stronger associations among frequent users. The authors suggest that smoke irritation and muscle relaxation in the throat may play a role.

articles.title: Challenges to political beliefs might engage brain networks tied to self-reflection, new study suggests
articles.summary: In a brain imaging study conducted in Poland, people with strong left-wing views barely changed their political beliefs after reading counterarguments, even as they lowered their confidence in factual claims. Their brains also responded differently to the two kinds of challenges.

articles.title: Playing video games with trusted friends may reduce addiction risks
articles.summary: Research reveals that playing video games with a trusted, familiar group of people can build player loyalty while simultaneously reducing the risk of video game addiction. A player's social environment heavily dictates their digital habits.

articles.title: Why do people with psychopathic traits enjoy fear? New psychology research offers a clue
articles.summary: Alfred Hitchcock argued that people enjoy fear only when they feel safe. A study suggests the idea may apply to people with psychopathic traits: a stronger sense of invincibility was linked to feeling less frightened by a horror clip.

articles.title: Scientists identify rare mutations in 36 genes that sharply raise the odds of OCD and tic disorders
articles.summary: A genetic study of nearly 4,000 people with OCD or tic disorders identified 36 genes in which rare damaging mutations sharply raise the odds of these conditions. Most of the genes appear to be shared between the two disorders.

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? articles.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
articles.summary: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not.

articles.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
articles.summary: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines.

articles.title: Popular cannabis sleep gummies may have a hidden dark side
articles.summary: A cannabis-derived ingredient commonly found in sleep gummies may be more habit-forming than previously thought, with new research showing that repeated exposure caused tolerance and withdrawal symptoms in mice. Scientists warn that CBN may carry risks similar to THC, although its long-term effects in humans remain largely unknown.

articles.title: Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and age-related damage.
